bib.title: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents

read.skipped: References (lines ~1086-2167) skimmed for lineage and keyword-scanned for instructions, not read line by line.

question: How is the evaluation of LLM-based agents organised, and what gaps remain?
contributions: Five-part analysis of agent evaluation: core capabilities, application-specific benchmarks, generalist agents, benchmark dimensions, evaluation frameworks
Table 1 comparing 8 benchmarks on data, environment, interface, metric, safety

results.claim: Many current agent benchmarks rely on coarse end-to-end success metrics that fall short in diagnosing specific agent failures; the survey calls for standardised trajectory-level metrics.
results.setup: Authors' judgement from the literature review; no measurement.
results.quote: Many current benchmarks rely on coarse-grained, end-to-end success metrics that, while useful for gauging overall performance, fall short in diagnosing specific agent failures.

results.claim: Of the 8 frameworks in Table 2, 3 (LangSmith, Google Vertex AI, AgentsEval) have a tick for trajectory assessment.
results.setup: Authors' own coding of 8 vendor evaluation frameworks; coding method and sources not stated beyond vendor documentation; the caption warns some capabilities are in initial phases.
results.table: Table 2, column Trajectory Assessment (ticks: LangSmith, Google Vertex AI evaluation, AgentsEval)
results.note: The text names only Vertex AI and LangSmith for trajectory assessment, then lists AgentEvals under reference-based modes. Count of 3 is derived from table ticks.

results.claim: Of the 8 representative benchmarks in Table 1, only TAU-Bench is marked Yes for safety.
results.setup: Authors' coding of 8 hand-picked 'representative' benchmarks (SWE-bench Ver., SWE-Lancer, Mind2Web, WebArena, PaperBench, TAU-Bench, AppWorld, GAIA); not a sample of the field.
results.table: Table 1, column Safety (only row TAU-Bench = Yes)

results.claim: Step-by-step judging assumes each action can be assessed in isolation and overlooks dependencies between steps; Galileo's action advancement metric is cited as a response.
results.setup: Stepwise evaluation as implemented in vendor frameworks (Arize Phoenix templates, etc.); authors' judgement.
results.quote: These approaches assume that each action can be meaningfully assessed in isolation, overlooking dependencies between steps.

results.claim: Reference-based trajectory evaluation is limited because multiple valid paths exist and writing references is often infeasible.
results.setup: LangSmith, Vertex AI, AgentEvals alignment modes: exact, partial, unordered, subset.
results.quote: However, reference-based methods are inherently limited, as multiple valid paths typically exist and manual reference specification is often infeasible.

results.claim: Evaluation frameworks overlook the cost of the evaluation itself when scaling over many traces with expensive LLM judges.
results.setup: Authors' judgement about the frameworks in Table 2.
results.quote: current frameworks overlook the cost incurred by the evaluation process itself, specifically when scaling over a large number of traces with expensive LLM judges.

results.claim: Cost and efficiency are often overlooked in agent evaluations; future frameworks should track token usage, API expenses, inference time.
results.setup: Authors' judgement; credits Kapoor et al. (2024b).
results.quote: Current evaluations often prioritize performance while overlooking cost and efficiency measurements.

results.claim: Robustness is often quantified via pass^k.
results.source: Yao et al. 2024 (tau-bench) by implication; the survey cites no source at this sentence
results.setup: Definition as given by the survey.
results.quote: Robustness is often quantified via pass^k, the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds across all k independent runs.

results.claim: Static environments such as the original Mind2Web miss compounding failures because wrong actions have no downstream consequences.
results.quote: incorrect actions have no down-stream consequences, missing compounding failures that can ultimately cause task failure.
results.note: PDF text has a line break after 'down-' ; quote to be matched as printed in the text.

results.claim: Most benchmarks conflate the backbone LLM with the agent harness.
results.setup: Authors' judgement; Harbor and Exgentic (the latter by the authors' group) cited as first steps.
results.quote: Most current agent benchmarks conflate two distinct evaluation targets

results.claim: SWE-bench Pro has 1,865 human-verified tasks over 41 repositories; model performance remains below 25% Pass@1.
results.setup: Reported second-hand; no model, date or harness named.
results.quote: Model performance remains below 25% Pass@1, highlighting current limitations in handling long-horizon, complex code changes.
results.note: Appendix E.2 says SWE-bench-pro SOTA 'hovers around 46%'; the two figures are not reconciled (no dates/models given).

results.claim: SWE-bench Pro state of the art hovers around 46%.
results.setup: Leaderboard snapshot, no model, metric or date named in the text.
results.quote: where current state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance hovers around 46%.

results.claim: SWE-bench Verified top performance now approximately 80%, suggesting near saturation.
results.setup: Leaderboard snapshot, no model or date named. SWE-bench Verified has 500 samples.
results.quote: with top performances now reaching approximately 80%, suggesting it is close to being saturated.

results.claim: WebArena top performance reached 74.3% as of April 19, 2026, from a February 2026 submission.
results.quote: as of April 19, 2026, top performance has reached 74.3%

results.claim: SWE-Lancer collected 1,400 freelance Upwork tasks with total payouts over $1M.
results.quote: SWE-Lancer (Miserendino et al., 2025) collected 1,400 freelance tasks from Upwork with total payouts over $1M.

results.claim: Deep research agents achieve 50-70% of human performance on Mind2Web 2 (judged by agent-as-a-judge).
results.quote: shows agents achieve 50 −70% of human performance

limits: Authors concede (Limitations): the survey is a snapshot of a fast-moving field; selection is representative not exhaustive; depth per benchmark is constrained; the future-directions list involves foresight and interpretation.
Appendix A describes keyword search over Google Scholar, ACL Anthology, HuggingFace Papers and arXiv, snowballing and expert consultation, but gives no count of papers found, screened or included.
Table 2 coding method and evidence are not stated; the caption says some capabilities are in initial phases.

Leaderboard figures (WebArena 74.3%, SWE-bench Verified ~80%, SWE-bench Pro ~46%) name no model or harness and will date; SWE-bench Pro is given as below 25% Pass@1 in Section 3.2 and around 46% in Appendix E.2.
No venue is printed in the PDF; the stamp is arXiv:2503.16416v2 [cs.AI] 23 Apr 2026.
Harbor and Exgentic, cited as steps toward decoupling LLM from harness, include the authors' group (Bandel et al. 2026a).
practices: Prefer dynamic over static environments so wrong actions have downstream consequences (Section 5).
Add guardrail metrics that penalise task success achieved through non-compliant actions (Section 5).
Track cost (tokens, API spend, inference time) as a core metric (7.2).
Vary LLM and harness independently in evaluation protocols (7.2).
Use WebArena for dynamic web, Mind2Web for static, SWE-bench Verified or SWE-bench Pro for coding, tau-bench for conversational, GAIA/AppWorld/OSWorld/HAL for generalist (Appendix E).

terms.definition: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds across all k independent runs
a.k.a. scaffold; the design of the agent around the backbone LLM
compare the trajectory against an expected optimal path, measuring alignment between observed and gold action sequences
